procedural_history.originating_court: Punjab High Court, sitting on the Circuit Bench at Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: An order dated 10-3-1960 (Annexure 'C' to the petition)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A single Judge of the Punjab High Court, sitting on the Circuit Bench at Delhi, allowed the Appellant's petition under Article 226. The Union of India appealed this decision to a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court via a Letters Patent Appeal (No. 97-D of 1965). The Division Bench allowed the appeal, overturning the single judge's decision.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant approached the Supreme Court after the Delhi High Court granted a certificate on 12-8-1968 for leave to appeal, primarily because the High Court held that the required test relating to valuation of the subject matter had been satisfied.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Division Bench erred in allowing an additional affidavit to be filed without affording the appellant an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit.

facts: During arguments before the Division Bench, a question arose as to whether the appellant's post of Editor had been abolished.
The Division Bench allowed the respondent (Union of India) to file an additional affidavit to clarify this point.
The appellant contended that this introduced a new case and that they were not given an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit to rebut its contents.
application: The Supreme Court found nothing in the judgment or the record to show that the appellant had ever asked for an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit and been denied.
The Court determined that the additional affidavit did not introduce a new case but merely clarified a position on an issue that was already before the court.

Specifically, the question of how the creation of the Central Information Service affected existing posts was already a part of the proceedings. The affidavit simply explained that the old posts ceased to exist when new ones were created in the revised grade.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the Division Bench did not err. The Court reasoned that the appellant never requested an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit, and the additional affidavit did not introduce a new case but only clarified an existing issue.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petition should have been dismissed on the ground of delay.

facts.fact: The petitioner's representation was first rejected on 29-07-1960, but the petition was not filed until 11-01-1963.
The Single Judge who initially heard the case was disposed to reject the petition on the ground of laches (delay).
However, the Single Judge overlooked the delay, following a precedent that the rule of delay can be relaxed after a petition is admitted if the case is 'positively good'.
A Division Bench, on appeal, was not inclined to interfere with the Single Judge's discretion in rejecting the objection based on delay.

application.law_application: The Supreme Court noted that the Division Bench had already declined to interfere with the Single Judge's decision on the matter of delay.
The Supreme Court then explicitly stated that it would not enter into the question of delay because the issue was not argued before it.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument to dismiss the petition on the ground of delay by declining to consider the issue, as it had not been argued before them, thereby leaving the lower courts' decisions on this point undisturbed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's case involved a demotion or reduction in rank, thereby attracting the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution.

facts: A new Central Information Service was created through rules promulgated under Article 309 of the Constitution, leading to a departmental reorganization.
The appellant, who held a temporary post as an Editor, was required to go through a selection process to be appointed to the new service.
Following the selection process, the appellant was appointed to a post of a lower grade (Assistant Editor).
The appellant's previous post of Editor was abolished and ceased to exist as part of this reorganization.
law: Article 311 of the Constitution provides protections against dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank for civil servants.
For Article 311 to apply to a reduction in rank, the action must be a punishment.
The rules for the new Central Information Service did not guarantee that candidates would be placed in a post with the same class, grade, or pay they held previously.
application: The Court determined that the appellant's change in post was not a demotion but a consequence of a departmental reorganization and the creation of a new service.
Since the post of Editor was abolished, the Court reasoned that there could be no question of demotion from a post that no longer existed.

The Court found nothing in the appointment order to suggest that the appellant was being demoted as a measure of punishment. The change was a result of a selection process for a new service, not a punitive action.

The Court also noted that the appellant's overall position had not necessarily worsened. He moved from a "precarious position of a temporary servant" to a permanent service, which improved his job security. He was also given the maximum pay in his new grade.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, concluding that his case did not involve a demotion or reduction in rank that would attract Article 311. The change in his post was a result of a bona fide departmental reorganization where his old temporary post was abolished, and he was appointed to a new permanent service through a selection process. The action was not a punishment, and his overall employment status arguably improved by gaining permanency.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned order violates Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant was in an officiating (temporary) appointment.
A new Central Information Service was created, and under its rules, the appellant was selected for a new post.
The impugned order terminated his officiating appointment and gave him a new, permanent appointment with a different designation.
The appellant argued this violated Articles 14 and 16 because the process did not have a similar effect on the position or rights of any other employee in the department.
law: Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution provide for the right to equality and equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
The application of a rule to the facts of individual cases is not expected to produce identically similar results in all cases.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the order terminated an officiating appointment, a position in which the appellant had no right to continue.
In its place, the appellant was given a fresh, permanent appointment, which improved his job security from a "precarious position" to a stable one.
The Court noted that the Selection Committee had considered the appellant's individual case and recommended the maximum pay in his new class and grade, which he received.
Therefore, the Court could not definitively say that the appellant's position had worsened on the whole.

The Court held that just because the process did not affect other employees in the same way did not constitute a violation of equality, as the results of applying a rule to individual cases cannot be expected to be identical.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's claim, concluding that the order did not violate Articles 14 or 16 of the Constitution because it moved the appellant from a temporary position to a permanent one, with the maximum pay for his new grade, and the fact that other employees were not affected similarly was not, by itself, a violation of equality.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Division Bench erred in allowing an additional affidavit to be filed without affording the appellant an opportunity to file a counter-affidavit.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the Division Bench should not have allowed an additional affidavit to be filed by the respondent without giving the appellant a chance to file a counter-affidavit in response.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as noted by the court, was that the appellant never asked for an opportunity to controvert the statements in the additional affidavit and therefore was not denied one.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petition should have been dismissed on the ground of delay.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the petition was not unduly delayed, as it was filed after the final rejection of his last representation, and therefore should not be dismissed on the ground of delay.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (Union of India) raised an objection that the petition should be dismissed due to delay (laches), as it was filed in 1963, a considerable time after the initial order in 1960.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant's case involved a demotion or reduction in rank, thereby attracting the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that his appointment to a Class II Grade III post was effectively a demotion or reduction in rank, which required adherence to the constitutional protections provided under Article 311.
respondent_arguments: The respondent would have argued that this was a fresh appointment based on the recommendation of the Union Public Service Commission, not a demotion, and therefore Article 311 was not applicable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the impugned order violates Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant likely argued that the order appointing him to the lower grade was arbitrary, discriminatory, and violated the principles of equality guaranteed by Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The respondent would have argued that the appointment process was fair, based on reasonable classification (such as 'Departmental candidates'), and followed the recommendations of the UPSC, thus not violating Articles 14 and 16.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order that terminates an officiating appointment, in which the employee has no right to continue, and offers a new appointment based on a selection process governed by a valid rule, is not considered a punishment or a reduction in rank. A rule is not void for a mere possibility of its misuse, and a court will not look behind a facially non-punitive order resulting from a fair and uniform process to find a hidden punitive motive.
obiter: The validity of a rule does not appear to have been assailed in arguments before the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant's appointment to a permanent Class II post, following the termination of his temporary officiating position in a higher grade, was not a demotion attracting Article 311, nor did it violate the equality provisions of Articles 14 and 16. This was because the change resulted from a fair and reasonable selection process for entry into a newly constituted service, where the appellant had no pre-existing right to the higher post, and his individual case was considered, resulting in benefits such as permanency and maximum pay in the new grade.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an action constitutes a 'reduction in rank' under Article 311, which depends on whether the employee had a right to the post from which they were moved.

Whether an administrative action violates Articles 14 and 16, which requires assessing if the process is arbitrary or results in unfair discrimination, or if it is based on a fair and reasonable procedure applied to individual cases.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to show that he had ever asked for an opportunity to controvert the additional affidavit and been denied that opportunity.

The court found that the impugned order terminated an officiating appointment in which the appellant had no right to continue, and therefore, it could not be considered a demotion or reduction in rank under Article 311.

The court rejected the argument that the order violated Articles 14 and 16, stating that a violation does not occur 'simply because the process which resulted in such an order did not have a similar effect upon the position or rights of any other servant in the Department.'

The court noted that the results of applying the selection rule 'could not be expected to be identically similar in all cases,' and that preferences based on honest assessments are not equivalent to punishment.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the rules had the effect of 'constituting a new service, with a fair and reasonable procedure for entry into it,' which was not a device to defeat Article 311.
The appellant was given a 'fresh appointment, with a different designation but permanent tenure and prospects,' which was seen as a benefit, not a punishment.
The Selection Committee had taken into account the 'special features of the petitioner's individual case' and recommended the 'maximum pay, in the class and grade of the post given to him.'

The appellant's position had not necessarily worsened on the whole, as 'from the precarious position of a temporary servant he had moved into a permanent service' and was 'no longer subject to the hazards of temporary employment.'
policy_considerations: Preferences due to honest assessments in a selection process, which are not above possibilities of error, have never been held to cast any reflection which could be equated with punishment.

The court affirmed the principle that the government can constitute a new service with a fair and reasonable procedure for entry, and the results of such a process will not be invalidated simply because they do not meet the expectations of some candidates.
